1. Introduction 
The purpose of this report is to provide a description of the experimental hardware and operations of 
used in the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project that is sufficient for 
informed interpretation of the experimental results. In contrast, it is not the intent of this document to 
review the project management, engineering development, design process, etc. although such aspects 
may be briefly addressed. 
 
The ACME suite of experiments are being carried out on the International Space Station (ISS) in the 
Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR). ACME features investigations with gaseous fuels, such as methane and 
ethylene.

tegrated Rack (CIR). ACME features investigations with gaseous fuels, such as methane and 
ethylene. In addition to the fuel state, the current ACME experiments use laminar, non-premixed (i.e., 
diffusion) flames for their studies. To simplify analysis, these flames are furthermore either axisymmetric 
or spherically symmetric, depending upon the experiment. 
 
Currently, ACME includes six independent experiments of which the first five were selected for testing in 
spaceflight by NASA while the sixth was selected by the Center for the Advancement of Science in Space 
(CASIS) and the National Science Foundation (NSF). 
 
The CIR facility was launched in 2008 and with the Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) was 
used for a series of liquid-fueled experiments from 2009 to 2017.

t Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) was 
used for a series of liquid-fueled experiments from 2009 to 2017. The facility was reconfigured and set 
up for ACME testing by the ISS crew in September and October 2017, where over 25 astronauts from 
Canada, Germany, Italy, Japan, Russia and the United States have thus far supported the project’s 
research. As of this writing, over one thousand ACME flames have been ignited on the ISS, where that 
began in Nov. 2017. It is expected that the planned ACME testing will be completed in 2021, when the 
CIR operations should subsequently shift to the Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction (SoFIE) project.

The CIR facility was preceded by the Combustion Module (CM) which flew on the space shuttle Columbia.

CIR facility was preceded by the Combustion Module (CM) which flew on the space shuttle Columbia. 
In 1997, the combustion research facility was within Spacelab on the STS-83 and STS-94 (Microgravity 
Science Laboratory) missions. It was subsequently reconfigured and flew in 2003 within SPACEHAB, again in 
the shuttle’s payload bay, in the STS-107 mission. The Combustion Module investigations included Laminar 
Soot Processes (LSP), Structure Of Flame Balls At Low Lewis-number (SOFBALL), and the Water-Mist Fire 
Suppression Experiment (Mist). Although all three experiments burned gaseous fuel, each had its own 
chamber insert, whereas ACME features a single modular chamber insert to accomplish multiple 
investigations.

A. General Description 
This section provides a general description of the ACME engineering from the ‘3.0 Experimental’ 
section of the following 2014 conference paper: 
Dennis P. Stocker, Fumiaki Takahashi, J. Mark Hickman, and Andrew C. Suttles, “Gaseous 
Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station,” Spring 
Technical Meeting of the Central States Section of the Combustion Institute, Tulsa, OK, 16–
18 March 2014.

As previously discussed, the ACME experiments will be conducted within the Combustion 
Integrated Rack (CIR) using a chamber insert, depicted in Figure 2, which was designed to 
accommodate gas delivery to a variety of exchangeable burners. Besides the chamber insert, 
other ACME-unique hardware includes a high-definition color camera and an avionics package, 
which is for data acquisition and control.

ACME’s chamber insert, which is ~0.4 m in diameter, provides common mounting for a variety of 
burners on the chamber axis (but only one at a time) and includes a retracting resistive igniter. As 
depicted in Figure 3, there will initially be gas-jet burners (with inner diameters ranging from 0.4 
to 3.2 mm), a small coflow burner (where the two concentric tubes have inner diameters of 2.1 
and 25 mm), porous spherical burners (with diameters ranging from 6.35 to 12.7 mm), and two 
flat porous burners for the BRE experiment (with inner diameters of 25 and 50 mm). Most burners 
will be equipped with a surface thermocouple, and each BRE burner will have two heat flux 
transducers.

l be equipped with a surface thermocouple, and each BRE burner will have two heat flux 
transducers. The internal pressure of the porous burners will be measured to allow monitoring 
of the pressure differential across the outlet surface. The igniter will have a crew-exchangeable 
tip and arm (to accommodate the various burners) and its stepper-motor drive will allow for 
precise positioning. 
 
 
Figure 3: ACME burner types, including from left to right, gas-jet burners, a co-flow burner, 
porous spherical burners, and flat porous burners for the BRE experiment. 
 
Ultimately, the spherical burners were limited to a single diameter of 6.35 mm, and the fabricated 
gas-jet burners were limited to two sizes with nominal inner diameters of 1.3 and 2.1 mm.

ricated 
gas-jet burners were limited to two sizes with nominal inner diameters of 1.3 and 2.1 mm. 
However, only the larger gas-jet burner was used during the spaceflight tests. The burners are 
addressed in detail in section 3.C. 
 
Unfortunately, the spherical burners have not always yielded spherically symmetric flames, 
presumably as a result of (1) greater burner flow through the joint between the porous sphere and 
supply tube, and (2) heat loss to the support tube (encompassing the supply tube) causing local 
flame quenching. 
 
Two types of igniter tips have been used during ACME testing. Most tests have been conducted 
using a loop igniter tip like those which had been successfully used in the droplet combustion 
experiments which preceded ACME research in the CIR.

en successfully used in the droplet combustion 
experiments which preceded ACME research in the CIR. However, some tests were conducted with 
a coil igniter tip, where that included the second round testing for both the Burning Rate Emulator 
(BRE) and Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame) experiments, with the 
exception of the latter’s first day testing. The CFI-G investigation will also use the coil igniter tip. 
For more information about the igniter tips, see section 3.D. 
 
The chamber insert includes three mass flow controllers (visible on the left of Fig. 2) for the 
delivery of fuel, oxidizer or inert (e.g., helium or carbon dioxide), and nitrogen to the burner. The

ivery of fuel, oxidizer or inert (e.g., helium or carbon dioxide), and nitrogen to the burner. The 
maximum fuel flow is 2 slpm (on a nitrogen basis), whereas much higher flows, e.g., 10 slpm (on 
a nitrogen basis), are possible for the oxidizer and nitrogen lines. The crew can exchange the mass 
flow controllers to provide appropriate ranges that maximize the flow accuracy. The gas delivery 
system enables on-orbit dilution of the fuel or oxidizer (but not both simultaneously), coflow,

inverse flames (e.g., oxidizer delivery to the center of a coflow burner), and premixed flames, 
although the latter are not planned for any of the current ACME experiments. Gases can also be 
delivered premixed to the space station where that is necessary in some circumstances, such as 
the blending of different fuel gases. CIR’s standard bottle sizes are 1, 2.25, and 3.8 liters but ACME 
will sometimes use smaller bottles as a hazard control to limit the deficient reactant (e.g., fuel)

Thus far, ACME tests were not conducted with carbon dioxide as a diluent. Furthermore, the fuel 
diluted with helium was premixed prior to launch rather than on orbit. Ultimately, oxidizer flows

diluted with helium was premixed prior to launch rather than on orbit. Ultimately, oxidizer flows 
of up to 20 slpm (on a nitrogen basis) were possible, while the nitrogen flow was limited to a 
maximum of 5 slpm. ACME has not used gas bottles smaller than 1 liter as indicated above; the 
bottle fill pressure was instead limited as an additional hazard control. 
 
ACME’s primary flame diagnostics are a suite of imaging systems including five video cameras and 
two illumination systems, of which three cameras are part of the CIR facility and are already in 
use on orbit. All but one of the cameras is mounted outside of the chamber. Collectively, the 
imaging systems will enable color, CH*, and OH* imaging; pyrometry; measurement of the soot 
volume fraction; and operational support.

CH*, and OH* imaging; pyrometry; measurement of the soot 
volume fraction; and operational support. However, it is unlikely that all functions would be 
exercised at any one time as will become apparent in the subsequent discussion. 
 
Color imaging is provided by two cameras: a high-definition digital camera mounted outside of 
the chamber and a standard analog camera mounted on the chamber insert (with a turning 
mirror). Both cameras are part of the ACME hardware that is now in development. The analog 
camera signal will be downlinked in near real time to support the experiment operations. Light-
emitting diodes within the chamber can be used to illuminate the igniter and burner to both 
support the operations and provide reference images. The 12-bit digital camera records at up to

h 
support the operations and provide reference images. The 12-bit digital camera records at up to 
30 full frames (1360x1024) per second, and is equipped with a motorized lens with independent 
control of the zoom, iris, and focus. The digital camera will be equipped with a filter assembly 
with four options, where selection of a clear “filter” allows for color imaging. Color imaging can 
also be carried out with a blue-green BG7 Schott glass filter, which balances the color planes to 
avoid saturation in the red while maintaining sensitivity in the blue and green. The natural flame 
color can be approximately reconstructed, but the primary purpose of the filter is pyrometry and 
measurement of the soot volume fraction, again via the techniques of [23-24]. Alternately, CH*

nd 
measurement of the soot volume fraction, again via the techniques of [23-24]. Alternately, CH* 
imaging can be conducted with this camera because the filter assembly includes a 430-nm 
bandpass filter with a 10-nm full width at half-maximum transmission (FWHM). A 450-nm 
bandpass filter (again with a 10-nm FWHM) can be used with the CH* filter to effectively subtract 
interfering broadband soot emission. However, the filter assembly rotates slowly so such 
subtraction effectively requires a separate test with each filter and of course reproducible flame 
conditions. 
 
The video from the analog operations (i.e., ops) camera, also referred to as the internal camera, 
is not archived in space. The video is instead recorded on the ground in the operations center. Its

Imaging of the dim hydrogen flames in the Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames

Imaging of the dim hydrogen flames in the Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames 
(s-Flame) experiment was particularly challenging with these, if not all, cameras. 
 
Pyrometry can alternately be accomplished with CIR’s monochrome High-Bit Depth Multispectral 
(HiBMs) camera, equipped with a Liquid-Crystal Tunable Filter (LCTF), which allows for imaging at 
multiple spectra, but requires a quasi-steady flame for measurement at each desired band. This 
camera has a telecentric optical system and is recorded at 512x512 and 30 frames per second 
(fps). Although it has a 1024x1024 pixel array, binning has been necessary because of signal loss 
through the LCTF. Both soot pyrometry and Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) are possible, where

loss 
through the LCTF. Both soot pyrometry and Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) are possible, where 
ACME is equipped with a crew-replaceable array of 5 silicon carbide (SiC) fibers. The fibers are 
orthogonal to the flame axis and the array can be translated along the flame axis to the desired 
position downstream of the burner, e.g., based on the downlink of the analog video. During set 
up, the crew can manually orient the array so that it is orthogonal to either ACME’s color digital 
camera or the HiBMs camera with the LCTF. An alternate fiber array including a platinum wire 
will be used for inflight characterization, which in combination with preflight calibration will 
enable determination of the soot volume fraction [24].

Thus far, TFP tests have been conducted with 14-micron fibers spaced apart by 5 mm for a total 
span of 20 mm (in the case of 5 intact ceramic fibers), neglecting optional translation of the array. 
Tests have been conducted using arrays with and without the platinum wire in the furthest 
downstream position. Tests have also been conducted with some of the fibers broken and

CIR has a second HiBMs camera, without a filter, that will be used in combination with CIR’s 
illumination package for alternate measurements of the soot volume fraction. This will be

During ACME operations, the HiBMs camera is typically archived at 15 fps because of data limits 
for transfer and downlink operations. And because operations are constrained by the data limits, 
image data from this camera are sometimes deleted without downlinking to enable additional 
testing. And in some testing, HiBMs images aren’t even acquired given their lesser value. 
 
Unfortunately, the HiBMs backlight illumination is significantly obstructed by the bracket for the 
electrode mesh further limiting its utility for the E-FIELD Flames experiment. This was a design 
trade-off necessitated primarily by ACME’s large number of cameras and other optical 
instruments.

CIR’s Low-Light-Level Ultraviolet (LLL-UV) package is a monochrome camera with an intensifier 
(for 280-700 nm) and a 310-nm bandpass filter (with a 10-nm FWHM) for OH* imaging. Again as 
a result of the signal loss through the filter, binning is employed such that the OH* images are 
recorded at 512x512 and 30 fps. 
 
During ACME operations, the LLL-UV camera has only been used for the Structure and Response 
of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame) experiment. 
 
While not discussed in the preceding section, another intensified camera was used throughout 
ACME testing, although its image data was sometimes deleted or not even acquired to allow the 
performance of additional tests.

by the arms of the Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) fiber array when it was moved inwards to the 
flame. More information about this camera can be found in its characterization report, CIR-RPT-

A third radiometer array was developed for the CFI-G experiment, where it is important to 
understand that only a single radiometer array can be used at a time. 
 
The narrow-view radiometers in the standard array are only fully sensitive in small spots, but they 
are each sensitive in a much greater Field of View (FOV) than represented in the preceding figure. 
They do not have lenses; their FOV is a result of an aperture where most of their FOV is within the 
penumbra which is only visible to a portion of the sensor. Figures representing the measured FOVs 
of the as-built standard and BRE radiometer arrays are found in section 3.F of this document.

Unfortunately, the radiometers in the BRE array typically saturated in the first round of BRE 
testing, so the standard array was used in its second round. However, those radiometers similarly 
saturated in many of round 2 tests. In this regard, each of ACME’s BRE and standard radiometers 
have a fixed gain. Meanwhile, each sensor in the radiometer array developed for the CFI-G 
investigation has two fixed gains, i.e., a high gain and low gain.

3. Spherical Burners 
The spherical burners have thus far been used for the CFI-G, Flame Design, and s-Flame 
experiments. In contrast to initial plans, spaceflight burners were only fabricated with a 
6.35-mm porous sphere. It was initially expected that flames which were more spherical 
might be generated with larger diameter porous spheres, but 2.2-s drop testing indicated 
that 6.35-mm diameter spheres were as good or better than the larger sizes in creating 
spherical flames.

-mm diameter spheres were as good or better than the larger sizes in creating 
spherical flames. 
 
Multiple copies of the spherical burner were launched to the ISS because of concerns that 
they might be damaged and/or might prove to yield flames which aren’t sufficiently 
spherically symmetric. 
 
The porous spheres were fabricated from sintering 316 stainless steel with 10-micron 
media grade, for which the porosity is approximately 41% and the density is 4.6 g/cm3. 
More specifically, each sphere was formed by sintering together sintered disks, where the 
supply tube should extend to the sphere’s center. Neglecting the interior of the supply 
tube, there is presumably no cavity within the porous sphere. 
 
Each sphere was furthermore sinter-bonded to its stainless-steel supply tube.

1. Overview 
The Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI-G) experiment is one of six independent experiments that 
make up the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project for which the tests were 
conducted within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station (ISS). 
 
The experiment’s Principal Investigator (PI) is Prof. Peter B. Sunderland of the Department of Fire 
Protection Engineering at the University of Maryland. The two Co-Investigators (Co-Is) are Profs. Richard 
L. Axelbaum and Forman A. Williams who are respectively from the Washington University of St. Louis and 
the University of California, San Diego (UCSD).

including CFI-G and the rest of the ACME investigations. In ACME’s preparatory drop testing, etc., Dr. 
Fumiaki Takahashi of the Case Western Reserve University (CWRU) served as the Deputy Project Scientist. 
For ACME’s spaceflight operations, the NASA science team included Drs. Uday G. Hegde and Vedha 
Nayagam who are also with CWRU. 
 
The ISS operations for CFI-G were conducted from March to Oct. 2021 in two sequential rounds of testing. 
The two rounds occurred during Increments 64-65 and 65-66 and respectively featured normal and 
inverse flames.

inverse flames. The inverse flame tests were conducted with the chamber filled with a mixture of nitrogen 
and gaseous fuel while an oxygen/nitrogen mixture flowed from the burner. As a result, the inverse 
flames were effectively inside out, e.g., where the soot formed outside rather than inside of the flames. 
Although it was in the second round, the final day of CFI-G testing was carried out in the normal flame 
configuration, with gaseous fuel (with or without nitrogen) flowing into an oxygen/nitrogen atmosphere. 
This was an added test day carried out under conditions in which low-temperature combustion occurred 
during the first round of testing.

CFI-G was a late addition to ACME, where the experiment was jointly selected for spaceflight by the 
National Science Foundation (NSF) and the Center for the Advancement of Science in Space (CASIS) rather 
than NASA. The selection was notably announced after the core ACME hardware had launched to the ISS 
and just weeks before ACME’s on-orbit operations began. It is effectively an extension of ACME’s Flame 
Design experiment for which the PI and Co-I are respectively Axelbaum and Sunderland. And it is likewise 
a follow-on to the Cool Flames Investigation (CFI), led by Williams, in which liquid droplets were burned 
rather than gaseous fuel.

2. Science Overview 
A. Background 
This background is the Project Summary from the experiment’s 2017 proposal in response to a 
solicitation from the NSF/CASIS Collaboration on Combustion and Thermal Transport Processes 
Research on the International Space Station to Benefit Life on Earth. 
 
Overview: 
Cool diffusion flames were discovered in 2012 aboard the ISS. This spawned a rapidly growing 
research field, but only a small number of measurements at limited conditions are available. 
Consequently, cool flame kinetics mechanisms cannot be adequately tested or advanced. This 
could be impeding the development of cleaner and more efficient internal combustion engines.

is 
could be impeding the development of cleaner and more efficient internal combustion engines. 
 
It is proposed here to observe cool diffusion flames supported by porous spherical burners fed 
with propane, n-butane, and n-pentane. Normal and inverse flames will be considered for a broad 
range of dilution conditions and pressures. The ISS is the ideal platform for observing cool 
diffusion flames because they typically require 20 s to establish and they could burn indefinitely. 
 
Tests will be performed using the ACME insert in the CIR. Minimal hardware development will be 
required because the spherical porous burners and gas delivery system will be those used by the 
Flame Design flight experiment, while the diagnostics will be those used by the CFI flight 
experiment.

esign flight experiment, while the diagnostics will be those used by the CFI flight 
experiment. 
 
The objectives are to observe diverse cool diffusion flames aboard the ISS, to simulate the tests 
with an advanced CFD model, and to identify or develop a chemical kinetics mechanism that 
accurately models these conditions. 
 
Intellectual Merit: 
Most internal combustion engines are designed using computer models that neglect cool flame 
chemistry, but ignition and flame propagation in engines depend on cool flame chemistry. Cool 
flame chemistry also has a significant impact on fuel octane and cetane numbers, whose 
understanding has large economic consequences. 
 
The proposed experiments will take advantage of many state-of-the-art diagnostics that are 
already available on the ISS.

nts will take advantage of many state-of-the-art diagnostics that are 
already available on the ISS. The flame system to be studied will allow steady spherical cool 
diffusion flames to be observed for the first time. An advanced CFD model will simulate the flames 
and will aid the testing and development of cool flame kinetics models. 
 
Observing cool flames burning as steady spherical diffusion flames will yield valuable insight into 
cool flame chemical kinetics. The measurements proposed cannot be performed in normal gravity 
or in ground-based microgravity facilities. 
 
Broader Impacts: 
The research will be disseminated widely to the combustion research community and to industry.

spherical, burner-supported diffusion flames. These one-dimensional flames offer a simple, 
fundamental configuration to improve the understanding of diffusion flame behavior and to 
explore such effects as transport, kinetics, soot formation, and radiation, which can be more 
pronounced under microgravity conditions (Atreya et al. 1992; Law et al. 2001; Lecoustre et al.

Spherically-symmetric flames are not generally practical in normal gravity. This can be explained 
by considering the Richardson number, which is the ratio of the buoyancy force to the inertial 
force,

Analytical work supports these observations of slow flame development. Radial velocities in 
spherical diffusion flames scale with 1 / r2, where r is radius. Thus, at only a few burner diameters 
distance from the sphere, diffusion is the dominant transport mechanism. The characteristic 
diffusion time is r2/D, where D is mass diffusivity. For r = 25 mm and D = 20 mm2/s, this diffusion 
time is 30 s. Decreasing the flame size can reduce this time, but will not permit the observation 
of radiative extinction followed by cool diffusion flames. Our analytical and numerical calculations 
indicate that approximately 30 s of jitter-free (less than 10-5 g) microgravity is needed to approach

icate that approximately 30 s of jitter-free (less than 10-5 g) microgravity is needed to approach 
quasi-steady state for these flames. The ISS is the only microgravity platform that can provide 
this environment.

C. Science Objectives 
The objectives text presented here is the ‘Hypotheses and Objectives’ section (1.3) of the 
experiment’s 2017 proposal in response to a solicitation from the NSF/CASIS Collaboration on

The hypotheses of this research are that testing aboard the ISS can demonstrate the following for 
the first time, contributing to an improved understanding of cool flame kinetics. 
1. Steady-state cool diffusion flames on spherical porous burners. 
2. Cool diffusion flames burning propane, n-butane, and n-pentane. 
3. Cool diffusion flames for a wide range of Zst, Tad, and pressures.

Abstract for Spherical Gas-Fueled Cool Diffusion Flames: An improved understanding of cool 
diffusion flames could lead to improved engines. CDFs are investigated here using a spherical 
porous burner with gaseous fuels in the microgravity environment of the International Space 
Station. Normal and inverse flames burning ethane, propane, and n-butane were explored with 
various fuel and oxygen concentrations, pressures, and flow rates. The diagnostics included an 
intensified video camera, radiometers, and thermocouples. Spherical CDFs burning gases were 
observed for the first time. However, these CDFs were not readily produced and were only

ses were 
observed for the first time. However, these CDFs were not readily produced and were only 
obtained for normal n-butane flames at 2 bar with an ambient oxygen mole fraction of 0.39. The 
hot flames that spawned the CDFs were 2.6 times as large. An analytical model is presented that 
combines previous models for steady droplet burning and the partial-burning regime for CDFs. 
The results identify the importance of burner temperature on the behavior of these CDFs. They 
also indicate that the observed CDFs reside in rich regions near a mixture fraction of 0.53. 
 
Abstract for Cool Diffusion Flames in a Stably Stratified Stagnation Flow: Cool diffusion flames 
have been a growing research topic since their discovery in 2012. Until now their study has been

have been a growing research topic since their discovery in 2012. Until now their study has been 
hindered by the high cost of the experimental systems used to observe them. A method is 
presented here for observing CDFs inexpensively using a pool of liquid n-heptane and parallel 
plates heated so as to produce a stably stratified stagnation flow. The flames were imaged with a 
color camera and measurements included gas phase temperatures, fuel evaporation rates, and 
formaldehyde emissions. These are the first observations of CDFs burning near the surface of fuel 
pools. The measured peak temperatures were between 705 – 760 K, which corresponds to an 
increase in gas temperature of 70 K. Autoignition first occurred at 550 K. Cantera autoignition

G. Impacts, Benefits, and Products 
Combustion provides 86% of the world’s energy and an even higher fraction of the energy used 
for transportation. The internal combustion engines used for transportation generally have 
thermal efficiencies of 38% or lower because of thermal losses. These efficiencies may increase 
to 60% if future engines can take advantage of ultra-lean combustion. However, this progress is 
being impeded by the limited understanding of the chemistry of cool flames. Research into cool

diffusion flames (whose peak temperatures are 500 – 1000 K) has grown exponentially since they 
were discovered in 2012. 
 
The measurements performed for this project will help to test and advance cool flame kinetics 
mechanisms. This should facilitate the development of more efficient internal combustion 
engines.

I. Introduction 
Tests for the Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI-G) experiment are conducted in the 
Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced 
Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. As explained in the research proposal: 
Cool diffusion flames were discovered during droplet experiments aboard the International 
Space Station (ISS) in 2012, and this initiated a rapidly growing field of combustion research. 
Droplet experiments necessarily involve unsteady burning rates, so cool diffusion flames have 
never been observed as steady spherical flames.

steady burning rates, so cool diffusion flames have 
never been observed as steady spherical flames. A natural progression toward understanding 
cool diffusion flames is to observe quasi-steady spherical flames on porous burners, and this 
is the topic of this proposal. The flames to be studied are rich in the physics and chemistry of 
combustion and thermal transport processes.

Most internal combustion engines are designed using computer models that neglect cool flame 
chemistry, but ignition and flame propagation in engines depend on cool flame chemistry. Cool 
flame chemistry also has a significant impact on fuel octane and cetane numbers, whose 
understanding has large economic consequences. 
 
The flame system to be studied will allow steady spherical cool diffusion flames to be observed 
for the first time. The tests, performed with gaseous fuel and a porous spherical burner, cannot 
be performed in normal gravity or in ground-based microgravity facilities.

Hypotheses 
The hypotheses of this research are that testing aboard the ISS can demonstrate the following 
for the first time, contributing to an improved understanding of cool flame kinetics. 
1. Steady-state cool diffusion flames on spherical porous burners.

3. Cool diffusion flames for a wide range of Zst, Tad, and pressures. 
4. Inverse cool diffusion flames. 
5. Cool diffusion flames for which a decrease in fluent flow rate will cause extinction, 
whereas an increase will cause a transition to a hot diffusion flame, with oscillation 
possible between hot and cool flames.

Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages 
over normal-gravity studies. For example, the natural flicker of flames, which is a buoyancy-
driven (i.e., gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity. 
Characteristic length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame 
structure.

ic length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame 
structure. Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion 
systems, can be studied at low velocities to simplify analysis. Microgravity flames tend to have a 
much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of 
characteristics than normal-gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment. 
The long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many 
microgravity flames are soot free. The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames 
advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important.

s 
advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important. 
For example, chemi-ion species, electronically-excited chemiluminescent species, are at very low 
concentration in typical flames, making the reduced buoyancy environment valuable for 
evaluating the minor species chemistry. With these advantages, microgravity testing can lead to 
new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the gravitational 
environment of the combustion application.

2. Any other difficulties in obtaining scientific data 
CFI-G’s two primary challenges are in initiating cool flames and discerning their 
presence. Based on the findings of the earlier studies with droplet combustion, non-
premixed cool flames can be directly by limiting the ignition energy or can occur after 
the self-extinguishment of (normal) hot flames. Tests intended to directly ignite cool 
flames sometimes unintentionally resulted in hot flames. 
 
A challenge for cool flame detection is concern about potential damage to the CFI 
intensified camera by exposing it to bright light, especially from the energized igniter, 
while the intensifier gain is set high.

Meanwhile, at high flow rates of fuel and nitrogen, the burner does not produce 
spherically symmetric flames. While nominally spherical at moderate flow rates, the 
flame’s center becomes increasing offset from the burner center. More specifically, 
the flame is shifted toward the supply tube indicating that the sintered attachment of 
the porous sphere to the supply tube is more ‘open’ than the pores of the spherical

E. Preliminary Research Findings [provided by the U. Maryland investigator team] 
The first three days of testing have yielded dozens of flames, some lasting several 
minutes. Based on the output from the photomultipliers, radiometers, and intensified 
camera images we do not believe any self-sustained cool flames were created. While it 
is possible that momentary cool flames were created, these are difficult to detect without 
increasing the gain on the intensified camera before the hot flames extinguish, which is 
planned.

V. Introduction 
Tests for the Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI-G) experiment are conducted in the 
Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced 
Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. As explained in the research proposal: 
Cool diffusion flames were discovered during droplet experiments aboard the International 
Space Station (ISS) in 2012, and this initiated a rapidly growing field of combustion research.

l 
Space Station (ISS) in 2012, and this initiated a rapidly growing field of combustion research. 
Droplet experiments necessarily involve unsteady burning rates, so cool diffusion flames have 
never been observed as steady spherical flames. A natural progression toward understanding 
cool diffusion flames is to observe quasi-steady spherical flames on porous burners, and this 
is the topic of this proposal. The flames to be studied are rich in the physics and chemistry of 
combustion and thermal transport processes.

Most internal combustion engines are designed using computer models that neglect cool flame 
chemistry, but ignition and flame propagation in engines depend on cool flame chemistry. Cool 
flame chemistry also has a significant impact on fuel octane and cetane numbers, whose 
understanding has large economic consequences. 
 
The flame system to be studied will allow steady spherical cool diffusion flames to be observed 
for the first time. The tests, performed with gaseous fuel and a porous spherical burner, cannot 
be performed in normal gravity or in ground-based microgravity facilities.

Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages 
over normal-gravity studies. For example, the natural flicker of flames, which is a buoyancy-
driven (i.e., gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity. 
Characteristic length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame 
structure.

ic length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame 
structure. Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion 
systems, can be studied at low velocities to simplify analysis. Microgravity flames tend to have a 
much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of 
characteristics than normal-gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment. 
The long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many 
microgravity flames are soot free. The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames 
advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important.

advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important. 
For example, chemi-ion species, electronically-excited chemiluminescent species, are at very low 
concentration in typical flames, making the reduced buoyancy environment valuable for 
evaluating the minor species chemistry. With these advantages, microgravity testing can lead to 
new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the gravitational 
environment of the combustion application.

Appendix M. Summary of the ISS data collection 
The CFI-G data is all digital and includes both image and non-image data, where this is true for the other 
ACME experiments. To be clear, there was no collection of soot or other physical samples that were 
subsequently transported to the ground. 
 
The CFI-G image data includes images from the following cameras: 
1. ACME DataCam, used with a clear fused-silica ‘filter’ and various zoom and focus settings (but 
those settings were consistent within each individual test) 
2. CFI intensified camera, used always (or at least nearly so) with a formaldehyde filter for CFI-G 
3. High-Bitdepth Multispectral (HiBMs) camera, equipped with a red filter corresponding to the

-G 
3. High-Bitdepth Multispectral (HiBMs) camera, equipped with a red filter corresponding to the 
opposing CIR illumination package, which was sometimes left off 
The raw DataCam images are in a Halcon Iconic Object (hobj) format, while the images from the CFI, and 
HiBMs cameras are provided in a Tagged Image File (tif) format. In contrast, the analog video was 
recorded on the ground in a Transport Stream (ts) format. 
 
The key non-imaging data from a test is a comma-delimited file that is described in detail in the Software 
Interface Design Description (ACME-DOC-010 Rev. D). 
 
The raw data is currently archived at NASA and work is underway to make it available publicly through 
NASA’s Physical Science Informatics System (PSI).

Droplets must be deployed free floating without any residual momentum in the center of the field of view of the CIR 
diagnostics. Diagnostics must be capable of recording the radiant emissions of both hot and cool flames. CIR must 
store be able to store digital imagery data from a full day of test point (approx. 8 burns) for later downlink.

1. Overview 
The CFI experiments are conceived as follow-up experiments to the FLEX and FLEX-2 droplet combustion experiments

ments are conceived as follow-up experiments to the FLEX and FLEX-2 droplet combustion experiments 
onboard the ISS to further explore the newly discovered quasi-steady “cool flames.” Cool flames are controlled by low 
temperature chemistry, and occur in the NTC region of n-alkane fuels. FLEX series of experiments showed for the first 
time that quasi-steady stable flames can be established surrounding a droplet in microgravity under certain conditions, 
without a visible flame at temperatures in the range of 700 to 900 K, unlike the hot flames where the flame temperature 
is higher than 1200 K. Since the cool-flame chemistry depends on the chemical structure of the fuel as well as pressure

. Since the cool-flame chemistry depends on the chemical structure of the fuel as well as pressure 
and temperature, three different fuel combinations were investigated, namely, pure n-dodecane, n-dodecane/iso-
dodecane mixtures and farnesane ( a renewable jet fuel) at ambient pressures up to 5 atmospheres. Cool flame 
extinction occurs when its static stability is lost close to the lower turnover point in the NTC region, addition of helium to 
the ambient gas is also considered. Results for droplet burning rates, flame dynamics, droplet extinction diameters, and 
flame radiant out put are measured.

3. Science Overview 
a. Background 
Understanding the combustion characteristics of liquid hydrocarbon fuels is of practical and fundamental 
importance. The United States alone consumes approximately 19 million barrels of liquid fuels per day, 
which averages out to an amazing 2.5 gallons per day per person. The primary reason for such high reliance 
on hydrocarbon fuels as the single most important energy source, not only in the US but in the rest of the

carbon fuels as the single most important energy source, not only in the US but in the rest of the 
world, is their high energy density, ease of handling, and portability, compared to many other forms of 
energy sources. With the emergence of newer technologies for internal combustion engines and the 
increasing use of renewable bio-fuels, such as the Homogeneous Charge Compression Ignition (HCCI) engine 
and bio-diesel, that promise cleaner more efficient and sustainable utilization of hydrocarbon fuels, the 
need to understand the fundamental chemical and physical aspects of liquid-fuel combustion is bound to 
increase. 
 
Commercially available transportation fuels, such as gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel, are comprised of many

ally available transportation fuels, such as gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel, are comprised of many 
hydrocarbon compounds, normal alkanes and branched alkanes being major components. The combustion 
characteristics of these alkanes are quite complex and follow branched-chain reaction pathways involving 
many intermediate radicals. The chemical pathways vary, depending on temperature and, to a lesser extent, 
on pressure. In general it is possible to identify a low-temperature reaction mechanism and a high-
temperature mechanism, with a transition region between them. Many hydrocarbons exhibit a unique 
feature in this transition region, namely that the reaction rate decreases with increasing temperature,

4 
 
leading it to be called the negative-temperature-coefficient (NTC) region. There area a number of models 
available in the literature, simplified chemical-kinetic model involving hundreds of reactions as well as 
detailed mechanisms involving thousands of reactions. 
 
Droplet-combustion experiments (FLEX, FLEX-2) conducted onboard the International Space Station, as part 
of the Flame Extinguishment Experiments, have revealed for the first time that large n-alkane droplets can 
continue to burn quasi-steadily in the NTC region (see, Fig 1). NTC behavior of the heat-release rate is 
necessary for low-temperature quasi-steady droplet burning to be stable. It was observed that the second-

ary for low-temperature quasi-steady droplet burning to be stable. It was observed that the second-
stage combustion of the droplet controlled by low-temperature NTC chemistry, referred to as ``cool-flame 
combustion" here for the sake of simplicity, abruptly ends at a finite droplet diameter, leaving the unburned 
droplet to vaporize in the hot atmosphere. A vapor cloud was also found to form around the droplet as the 
partially oxidized fuel condensed immediately following cool-flame extinction.

Furthermore, the second-stage flame is shown to lie closer to the droplet surface where the rates of heat 
generation by the NTC chemistry is dynamically balanced by the heat loss rate. Unlike the hot-flame 
combustion where the overall process is controlled by equilibrium thermodynamic properties of the fuel, 
the cool-flame combustion depends on the chemical-kinetic details of the NTC region. These experimental 
and numerical studies provide a new tool to further explore the NTC chemistry of liquid fuels in an entirely 
new way. The experimental cool-flame droplet burning rates provide measures of the heat-release rates

way. The experimental cool-flame droplet burning rates provide measures of the heat-release rates 
and stoichiometry, the flame-diameter evolution provides insight into hot-flame diffusive and convective 
heat-loss effects, and the droplet extinction diameter provides a stringent measurement of chemical-kinetic 
characteristic times. 
 
The objectives of the CFI experiments is to further explore the cool flame phenomenon using pure fuels, and 
fuel mixtures over a range of pressures and helium dilution. 
 
b. Rational for Microgravity (if unusual)

5 
 
Rationale for microgravity remains the same for all the droplet combustion experiments conducted onboard 
the ISS. In microgravity the droplets burn in a spherically symmetric form, and therefore it is possible to 
model the processes with complex chemical kinetic mechanisms involving thousands of reactions leading to 
a better understanding of the chemistry. Moreover, the cool flames need much longer residence times and 
cannot be observed under normal gravity conditions with droplet flames.

c. Anomalies That Effect Science Surprises/New Discovery 
No new anomalies or surprises were observed during the CFI experiments. However, as the ambient 
pressure is increased above 2 atm, multiple reignition cycles were observed, where first the hot flame

sure is increased above 2 atm, multiple reignition cycles were observed, where first the hot flame 
extinguishes due to radiative heat loss followed by cool flame, and then reignition to a hot-flame followed 
by a cool flame, with this cycle repeating several times until the fuel droplet is completely consumed. This 
behavior is unexpected based on earlier observations from FLEX experiments. Furthermore, the soot-shell

which surrounds the droplet and lies between the droplet surface and the flame, became unstable and ill-

5.3 Cool flame extinction:

8 
 
Cool flame extinction is controlled primarily by chemical kinetics. As the droplet size decreases, the residence 
time in the reaction zone of the gas-phase diffusion flame is reduced to a value corresponding to which the cool 
flame becomes statically unstable, and this leads to cool flame extinction. Figure 4 shows the cool flame 
extinction diameter as function of ambient pressure for both free-floated and fiber-supported droplets for pure 
n-dodecane burning in air. As mentioned earlier, as the pressure is increased above approximately 2 atm, 
reignitions were commonly observed, eventually leading to complete combustion of the fuel droplet. It is 
interesting to note that the 40 micron fiber shows relatively little effect on the extinction diameter.

Since the cool flame extinction is an instability phenomenon where the dynamic balance between heat release 
and heat loss from the flame is lost at the lower turning point in the NTC region, one would expect addition of 
helium to have a substantial influence on the process. Figure 5 illustrates the effect of helium dilution on the 
extinction diameter for n-dodecane. Increase helium dilution leads to earlier cool flame extinction giving a larger 
extinction diameter.

5.4 Sooting behavior as function of ambient pressure: 
The effects and the process of soot formation during cool flame combustion remains largely unexplored. The 
shoot shell that forms during hot flame is stabilized by the balance of force between fluid mechanical drag 
and the thermophoretic force. At low pressures a stable spherical soot-shell is formed. However, as the 
pressure increase the soot-shell becomes diffuse and undefined. The reasons for this phenomenon is still 
not well understood. At low pressures, due to the low flame temperature of the cool flame, soot is not 
formed.

derstood. At low pressures, due to the low flame temperature of the cool flame, soot is not 
formed. The soot that is formed during the hot flame combustion is simply convected away from the droplet 
surface. But, when the pressure increases, residual soot is seen surrounding the droplet even after the hot 
flame extinction. The mechanisms behind this process has not been fully understood, and further analysis 
and research is needed.

1 INTRODUCTION 
 
The Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment (SPICE) Investigation will be operated onboard the 
International Space Station (ISS) in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG). A previous 
version of the SPICE design was called the Enclosed Laminar Flames (ELF) experiment, which 
flew in the Middeck Glovebox on the Space Shuttle STS-87. The Enclosed Laminar Flames 
(ELF) experiment objective was to study fundamental phenomena related to the mechanisms 
controlling the stability and extinction of jet diffusion flames. The design modifications made as 
a result of a carrier change (Middeck GBX to ISS MSG) are considered significant enough that

e as 
a result of a carrier change (Middeck GBX to ISS MSG) are considered significant enough that 
the SPICE Hardware is not considered Series Flight Hardware of the original ELF design. 
 
This Phase III Flight Safety Data Package (SDP) documents the hazards assessed for SPICE. 
This SDP documents compliance to NSTS/ISS 1700.7B and is prepared in accordance with 
NSTS/ISS 13830C. A brief overview of the experiment hardware and MSG interfaces is 
presented first, followed by a brief description of crew procedures. Finally, a safety assessment 
of SPICE Hazards is presented. Hazards that have not been eliminated by design have been 
addressed and documented in the Standard Hazard Form (JSC 1230 Form) or in a Unique 
Hazard Report (JSC 542B Form).

1.3 EXPERIMENT OVERVIEW 
 
The predecessor investigation to Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment (SPICE) was called 
Enclosed Laminar Flames (ELF) and was developed by NASA/GRC for flight on the Shuttle 
Spacelab during the Fourth United States Microgravity Payload (USMP-4 / STS-87) mission in 
November 1997. 
 
SPICE continues to study fundamental phenomena related to understanding the mechanisms 
controlling the stability and extinction of jet diffusion flames. SPICE will stabilize an enclosed 
laminar flame, measure the overall flame shape to validate the theoretical and numerical 
predictions, measure the flame stabilization heights, and measure the temperature field to verify

predictions, measure the flame stabilization heights, and measure the temperature field to verify 
flame structure predictions. 
 
The differences in ELF and SPICE hardware are the following: 
 
 
The Gas Bottle Assembly size increased from 75 ml to 150 ml, and maximum pressure 
was reduced from 350 psi to 230 psi. ELF bottles were open on both ends with a plug placed in 
one end and the valve in the other. For SPICE only one end of the bottle has an opening. 
 
 
The original fuel was 50/50 % methane. Propane, Ethylene, Propylene have been added 
as fuels. The increase in bottle size and decrease in pressure cause the worst case SPICE 
bottle to have three times the energy of an ELF bottle due to fuel. Also the number of bottles 
increased from 6 to 12.

s the energy of an ELF bottle due to fuel. Also the number of bottles 
increased from 6 to 12. 
 
 
 For the Experiment Assembly (EA) the Mass Flow Controller model was changed. 
 
 
There is a new Electronics power video box power box, a new video camera, a new still 
camera and there is an interface with MSG video drawer.

flight.

1.5.6 MSG Working Volume and Air Filtration System 
The SPICE experiment combustion process is run with the MSG Working Volume configured in 
the normal mode (MSG Fans on lowest setting) with the side loading ports and glove ports 
installed. This mode provides one level of containment for combustion by-products (all by-
products are tox level 0). At the end of the combustion process the MSG fans maybe changed 
to a higher speed and run for a 5-minute period in order to re-circulate the Working Volume air 
and clean-up combustion byproducts using the Working Volume Air Filtration System.

SPICE hardware is designed to meet the expected launch, on-orbit and return loads specified in 
MSFC-RQMT-2888, Paragraph 3.1.1.1, and Table 1 which is consistent with SSP 57000 
requirements. The stowage loads in MSFC-RQMT-2888 are based on a worst case condition of 
the Middeck and MPLM stowage loads. SPICE hardware will be stowed in soft transfer bags 
and transported in the MPLM for transfer to the ISS. All the SPICE hardware will be soft stowed 
for return. ZIN Tech Engineering has performed an analysis of test levels specified in NASA-
STD-7001 (NASA Payload Vibration Test Criteria) and MSFC-RQMT-2888 to define vibration

2.1 SPICE Science and Hardware Overview: SPICE continues to study fundamental phenomena to

2.1 SPICE Science and Hardware Overview: SPICE continues to study fundamental phenomena to 
understand the mechanisms controlling the stability and extinction of jet diffusion flames. SPICE will 
stabilize an enclosed laminar flame, measure the overall flame shape to validate the theoretical and 
numerical predictions, measure the flame stabilization heights, and measure the temperature field to 
verify flame structure predictions. The objective of the SPICE experiment is to find the laminar 
smokepoint properties of nonbuoyant jet diffusion flames (i.e., the properties of the largest laminar jet 
diffusion flames that do not emit soot) for several fuels under different nozzle diameter/ co-flow velocity 
configurations.

not emit soot) for several fuels under different nozzle diameter/ co-flow velocity 
configurations. Luminous flame shape measurements would also be made to verify models of the flame 
shapes under co-flow conditions. The soot point is a simple measurement that has been found useful to 
study the influence of flow and fuel properties on the sooting propensity of flames. This information 
would help support current understanding of soot processes in laminar flames and by analogy in 
turbulent flames of practical interest. Unfortunately, while the laminar smoke-point properties of 
buoyant jet diffusion flames at normal gravity (ng) are well known, corresponding information for 
nonbuoyant flames is limited and questionable. Thus, the measurements of the laminar smoke-point

nonbuoyant flames is limited and questionable. Thus, the measurements of the laminar smoke-point 
properties proposed here would also reduce the risk of future experiments involving hydrocarbon-fueled 
laminar jet diffusion flames in spacecraft.

Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment (SPICE) 
Abstract 
The laminar smoke point is the condition (and the luminous flame length) where a flame begins 
to emit soot. Smoke points indicate the sooting propensity of a fuel in diffusion flames. In normal 
gravity, laminar smoke points have been measured for many gaseous and condensed fuels. 
Laminar smoke points have been found to correlate with soot volume fractions and radiative loss 
fractions of turbulent diffusion flames. SPICE project measured laminar smoke points in non-
buoyant laminar jet diffusion flames in co-flowing air aboard the International Space Station. 
Fifty-two smoke points were found for ethylene, propane, propylene, and propylene/nitrogen 
mixtures.

ifty-two smoke points were found for ethylene, propane, propylene, and propylene/nitrogen 
mixtures. Burner diameters were 0.41, 0.76, and 1.6 mm and co-flow velocities varied from 5.4 – 
65 cm/s. These flames afford extensive control over residence time via variations in dilution, 
burner diameter, and co-flow velocity. Increasing co-flow velocity decreases luminous flame 
lengths, but moves smoke points to higher fuel flow rates and longer luminous flame lengths. 
Smaller burners have longer smoke points for co-flowing flames. These trends can be explained 
qualitatively by considering total residence time effects. The luminous flame lengths generally 
correlate with fuel mass flow rate divided by stoichiometric mixture fraction, although they

ally 
correlate with fuel mass flow rate divided by stoichiometric mixture fraction, although they 
increase slightly as air velocity decreases. The measured smoke point lengths were found to 
correlate with burner diameter to the –0.91 power times coflow velocity to the 0.41 power. The 
measurements allow estimates of pseudo threshold soot indices (TSI) for microgravity diffusion 
flames, indicating an unusually high sooting propensity for propane in microgravity. A model of 
residence times in coflowing flames is developed, and although residence time helps explain 
many of the observations, it does not correlate the measured smoke points. The measurements 
yielded estimates of sooting propensities of the present fuels in microgravity diffusion flames.

Soot formation in hydrocarbon-fueled flames is an important unresolved problem in combustion 
science. Soot is estimated to be responsible for up to 52,000 premature deaths annually in the U.S.1 
and is believed to contribute to climate change and glacial melting.2 Radiation from soot in flames is 
beneficial in many applications but also contributes to unwanted heat loads in engines and the spread 
of fires.

n many applications but also contributes to unwanted heat loads in engines and the spread 
of fires. Carbon monoxide emitted by smoking flames is the major cause of death in fires.3 
Knowledge of Soot formation is needed for developing computational combustion.

2 
 
The differences between soot processes in buoyant and nonbuoyant laminar jet diffusion flames can 
be seen by comparing their soot production regions as plotted in Fig. 1. Soot formation in diffusion 
flames generally is limited to fuel-equivalence ratios, φ, in the range 1-2, which are marked on the 
plots. Unlike gases, which both convect and diffuse, soot mainly convects with the flow velocity so 
that it moves along the streamline. For buoyant flames, the dividing streamline generally is inside 
the soot formation region so that most of the soot initially forms near the flame sheet, where φ, =1, 
and then moves radially inward toward cooler regions having higher fuel concentrations. The soot

and then moves radially inward toward cooler regions having higher fuel concentrations. The soot 
formation process for nonbuoyant flames is completely different: most of the soot initially forms 
near the cool core of the flame, where φ is close to 2, and is drawn directly toward the flame sheet. 
Results from an MSL-1 combustion project, the Laminar Soot Processes (LSP), revealed that the 
smoke height phenomenon in microgravity can be substantially different form that seen in normal 
gravity. The removal of buoyancy induced acceleration can cause the smoke point phenomenon to 
be dominated by radiative heat losses for conditions of low overall flame velocity. Under these 
conditions the flame extinguishes at the flame tip allowing soot to be emitted. In spite of this effect,

ions the flame extinguishes at the flame tip allowing soot to be emitted. In spite of this effect, 
it is still possible to have flames that either emit soot along all stream lines or do not emit soot 
anywhere, for conditions where radiation losses do not dominate.

The information of smoke-point properties and flame shapes is needed to improve our understanding 
of heat and mass transfer mechanisms for different flame conditions. Unfortunately, while the 
laminar smoke-point properties of buoyant jet diffusion flames at normal gravity are well known, 
corresponding information for nonbuoyant flames is limited and questionable. Thus the insights of

corresponding information for nonbuoyant flames is limited and questionable. Thus the insights of 
soot generation and oxidation processes under microgravity conditions are critical to devise better 
fire safety strategy in spacecraft needed for long term space travels and other space exploration 
activities. In addition, the improved understanding of soot processes in laminar flames will help us, 
by analogy, to gain better understanding of soot processes in practical turbulent flames. 
 
 
The objectives of the SPICE experiments is to find the laminar smoke-point properties of non-
buoyant jet diffusion flames for several fuels under different nozzle diameter/co-flow velocity 
configurations. Luminous flame shape measurements would also be made to verify models of the

3 
 
flame shapes under co-flow conditions. In particular, the experiments are planned to be conducted 
under the following conditions: six types of fuels: methane, ethylene, propane, propylene, 75% 
propylene mixed with 25% nitrogen in moles, and 50% propylene mixed with 50% nitrogen in moles; 
three nozzles: 0.4, 0.8 and 1.6 mm ID and two air velocities: 100% and 50% of the maximum air 
flow velocity (near 50cm/s). The operation procedures are as such that the air velocity is set first, 
then start the fuel flow and ignite the flame. Fuel flow rate is adjusted until the smoke point is 
reached. Thus, for each combination of a fuel and a nozzle size, two smoke point fuel flow rates are 
obtained. One is under 100% air velocity and the other is under 50% air velocity. Then in the case of

50% air velocity, the fuel flow rate is reduced to 50% of the smoke point fuel flow rate to get a flame

especially those with high air velocity, large burners, and long flames, and is attributed to coflow 
perturbations. This increased slightly the uncertainties in smoke points for these conditions.

The sooting propensity of the present fuels, identified from the smoke point lengths for fixed burner 
diameter and coflow velocity, generally increases from propane to ethylene, to 50% propylene, to

DISCUSSION 
 
Although it is convenient to classified all flames, laminar vs. turbulent and diffusion vs. premixed, 
into two categories based on their soot emission conditions, i.e., soot emitting flames and non-soot 
emitting flames, the conditions delineating the two or the conditions of onset of soot emission are 
difficult to define. Up to date, these conditions have been documented solely based on experimental 
observations. Many efforts have been made to develop a universal method of defining the onset of 
soot emission, i.e., smoke point, conditions, in terms of primary parameters of the flame. But none of 
these efforts has been quite successful yet. The primary parameters of the flame mentioned here refer

se efforts has been quite successful yet. The primary parameters of the flame mentioned here refer 
to parameters used to set the flame, not those generated by the flame. The primary parameters of jet 
diffusion flames include fuel type, fuel and oxidizer supply rates, ambient temperature and pressure, 
and configuration of the device where the flame takes place, such as nozzle diameter and dimensions 
of the combustion chamber. The flame temperature, gas velocity and species distributions as well as 
flame shapes and derived parameters such as heat generation and heat loss, are the parameters 
generated by the flame which is not considered as primary parameters. If a method that relates 
smoke point to those primary parameters were found, we would be able to predict whether a flame

emits soot or not based on the planned flame conditions. In the course of pursuing such a universal 
method, a number of surmises of the mechanism of soot emission have been proposed to associate 
smoke point with certain flame generated parameters. Those surmises served as a middle step in 
hoping to help further development of the aforementioned method. The first surmise, and least 
controversial, is that smoke points occur when soot temperature drops below a critical temperature 
prior to soot burnout. This temperature is about 1300 K in normal gravity8,9 and 1000 K in 
microgravity.10,11 The second is that smoke point occurs when radiative loss fraction reaches 0.2 –

icrogravity.10,11 The second is that smoke point occurs when radiative loss fraction reaches 0.2 – 
0.4 for normal-gravity flames12-16 or 0.4 – 0.6 for microgravity flames.17 Since the radiative fraction 
of heat loss increases with fuel flow rate, smoke point will occur as the fuel flow rate is higher than

CLOSING REMARKS 
Smoke points of 55 microgravity gas-jet diffusion flames in coflowing air were measured in earth 
orbit. The conditions emphasized small burners and the effects of coflow velocity. These flames 
allow extensive control over residence time, which is important in smoke point phenomena. The 
major conclusions are as follows: 
1. An increase in coflow velocity increases the smoke point length. 
2. A decrease in burner diameter increases the smoke point length. 
3. These two effects can be explained qualitatively by considering residence times; increased 
fuel and/or coflow velocities yield increased smoke point lengths.

4. The sooting propensities of the present fuel mixtures in microgravity increase according to 
ethylene < propane < 50% propylene < 75% propylene < propylene. This is the same as in 
normal gravity except for the exchanged positions of ethylene and propane. 
5. Consistent with past theory and experiments, luminous length at the smoke point is 
proportional to fuel mass flow rate. However there is a slight increase in luminous length as 
ua / uf decreases. 
6. Although residence time is helpful in understanding the present smoke points, it does not 
yield quantitative correlations of smoke points.
